stories.headline: US STRIKES IRAN FOR A SIXTH STRAIGHT NIGHT AS OIL JUMPS 4% AND THE DOLLAR, NOT GOLD, BECOMES THIS WEEK'S SAFE HAVEN
stories.body: US Central Command carried out a sixth consecutive night of airstrikes on Iranian military and logistics targets, sending WTI up 4.00% to $82.11 a barrel and Brent up 2.04% to $85.95, both near one-month highs, as Hormuz shipping traffic thinned and Tehran signaled the Houthis could move to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The S&P 500 fell 1.01% to 7,457.69 while investors rotated into the dollar rather than gold, with the DXY holding near 100.78.
stories.explain: Oil chokepoint risk gets priced into futures the moment a threat becomes credible, since roughly a fifth of global oil consumption transits Hormuz and rerouting options shrink further once Bab el-Mandeb is also in play - that's why crude jumped before a single extra barrel actually stopped moving. The dollar, not gold, is absorbing this week's safe-haven flows because the same oil shock that raises war risk also lifts US inflation expectations and trims bets on near-term Fed cuts, which supports a yield-bearing currency more than a zero-yield metal.

stories.headline: CHIP STOCKS SLIDE TOWARD A BEAR MARKET AS CHINA'S KIMI K3 AND A NETFLIX MISS DEEPEN THE NASDAQ SELLOFF
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.49% to about 28,592.66 as the semiconductor group extended its worst weekly rout since last year's tariff selloff, down roughly 20% from its record on doubts that AI infrastructure spending can keep justifying current valuations. Chinese startup Moonshot's new Kimi K3 model, competitive with leading US models, compounded the unease, while Netflix shares fell more than 10% after revenue of $12.56 billion narrowly missed the $12.6 billion consensus despite an EPS beat.
stories.explain: Chip stocks trade on the market's confidence that hyperscaler capex converts into durable revenue, so evidence that a Chinese competitor can match frontier AI performance for less directly threatens the pricing power baked into demand forecasts for that capex. Netflix's tiny revenue miss drew an outsized 10% punishment because at its valuation the market was pricing near-flawless execution, and a roughly $40 million shortfall against a $12.6 billion consensus was enough to break that assumption.

stories.headline: GOLD HEADS FOR ITS WORST WEEK SINCE JUNE EVEN AS IRAN AIRSTRIKES INTENSIFY
stories.body: Gold slipped to about $3,980 an ounce, down roughly 0.3% on the day and 3.4% for the week - its steepest weekly drop in six weeks - even as US strikes on Iran entered a sixth night. Silver fell alongside it to an eight-month low, with both metals losing out to the dollar as this week's preferred safe-haven trade.
stories.explain: Gold usually rallies on exactly this kind of shock, but it's losing a tug-of-war with two forces working against it: a firmer dollar pulling safe-haven flows its own direction, and oil-driven inflation expectations that make traders less confident the Fed keeps cutting, which raises the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yield asset. When a safe-haven asset falls during a genuine geopolitical escalation, it usually means a competing asset - here, the dollar - is absorbing the flows that would otherwise go to it.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD EASES TO 4.55% AS TRADERS PRICE JUST A 12% CHANCE OF A JULY HIKE, BUT THE OIL SHOCK CLOUDS THE PATH
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped about 3 basis points to 4.55% and the 2-year eased to 4.18% after this week's cooler June CPI left futures markets pricing roughly a 12% probability of a Fed hike this month and about 56% by September. That calm is now colliding with a fresh oil shock: WTI's 4% jump on the Iran conflict threatens to reverse the disinflation narrative that pulled yields lower in the first place.
stories.explain: Cooler CPI normally pulls yields down because it raises the odds the Fed can hold or cut instead of hike, and today's move follows that script. But a sustained oil shock works through the same inflation channel in reverse - energy costs feed directly into headline CPI and into transportation costs economy-wide - so if crude's rally holds, the same data that just talked yields lower could reverse course within a month or two, which is exactly the tension the market is now pricing into the curve.

stories.headline: LOUISVILLE LANDS TWO OF THE PORTAL'S BEST IN FLORY BIDUNGA AND JACKSON SHELSTAD AS PAT KELSEY RELOADS
stories.body: Louisville added Kansas big man Flory Bidunga, 247Sports' top-ranked player in the transfer portal, and Oregon guard Jackson Shelstad in the same week, giving Pat Kelsey two of the cycle's most coveted transfers as the Cardinals push to build on last season's run. Elsewhere, in a portal window now compressed to 15 days from 30 a year ago, Kansas added former Utah forward Keanu Dawes (12.5 ppg, 8.8 rpg) and Duke landed former Wisconsin guard John Blackwell, who averaged 19.1 points on a 59.3% true shooting mark last season.

stories.headline: CLIPPERS RALLY PAST TIMBERWOLVES IN OVERTIME TO REACH THE NBA SUMMER LEAGUE CHAMPIONSHIP GAME
stories.body: The Clippers beat the Timberwolves 128-120 in overtime behind Keaton Wagler's 26 points and Sean Pedulla's 24 points and 11 assists in the semifinal, sending Los Angeles to Sunday's championship game on ESPN. The result caps a Summer League in which LeBron James has told the Lakers he won't return for 2026-27 and Victor Wembanyama became eligible to negotiate a five-year, $252 million rookie extension - the richest in Spurs history.

stories.headline: NFL SUSPENDS CARDINALS SCOUTING EXECUTIVE RYAN GOLD INDEFINITELY FOR LEAKING 2026 DRAFT PICKS AND GAMBLING
stories.body: The league suspended Arizona's director of college scouting, Ryan Gold, indefinitely after finding he shared confidential 2026 draft-selection information before picks were announced and placed parlay bets on NFL and college games; the NFL says it found no evidence any other Cardinals staffer, coach or player was involved. Separately, Tennessee signed DT Jeffery Simmons to a three-year, $105.8 million extension with $100 million guaranteed, making him the highest-paid defensive tackle in NFL history and resetting the position's market well above Chris Jones's prior $31.8 million-a-year mark.

stories.headline: SEC MEDIA DAYS OPEN MONDAY IN TAMPA WITH LANE KIFFIN'S LSU DEBUT AND SIX NEW HEAD COACHES HEADLINING
stories.body: The four-day SEC Media Days kick off Monday in Tampa - the conference's first time hosting there - with Lane Kiffin appearing for the first time as LSU's coach after leaving Ole Miss mid-Playoff-run, part of a six-new-coach class that also includes Kentucky's Will Stein and Florida's Jon Sumrall. The event arrives as the SEC moves to nine conference games in 2026 and enters its fourth straight season without a national title, with Texas's Steve Sarkisian among the coaches already facing hot-seat scrutiny.

sports.detail: No game until the Apple Cup opener vs. Washington State, now moved to Sunday, Sept. 6 (1 p.m. PT, NBC). Jedd Fisch's staff has added a 4-star cornerback, its highest-rated 2026 commitment, along with a 4-star safety, as it builds toward year two in Seattle.

Washington is one of four finalists for 5-star guard Dylan Mingo as Danny Sprinkle's staff continues rebuilding around a heavy international pipeline, headlined by Croatian forward Boris Tisma. Jasir Rencher looks healthy - shooting, driving and lifting - in offseason workout footage.

Rookies reported to training camp Friday, led by first-round RB Jadarian Price, who projects for a heavy workload - including kick returns - after Kenneth Walker left in free agency and Zach Charbonnet's ACL recovery continues. Veterans and nine public practices begin July 25 in Renton, with Football Fest set for Aug. 8 at Lumen Field.

Detroit's Summer League ended Friday in a 101-87 loss to Miami after blowing an 11-point halftime lead, getting outscored 35-15 in the fourth. Ebuka Okorie led the Pistons with 27 points as Detroit finished 1-4 in Las Vegas; the offseason additions of John Collins (3 yrs, $51M) and a trade for Jrue Holiday remain the bigger story ahead of training camp.

Seattle fell 7-0 to San Francisco on Friday as Willy Adames hit a grand slam and Landen Roupp threw seven sharp innings for the Giants. The Mariners (48-49, 2nd in the AL West, holding a wild-card spot) host the rematch tonight at T-Mobile Park, first pitch 5:08 p.m. PT, Bryan Woo vs. Logan Webb.

watchlist: Mariners host Giants tonight, 5:08 p.m. PT at T-Mobile Park - Woo vs. Webb after Friday's 7-0 loss
NBA Summer League championship game Sunday, 9 p.m. ET on ESPN - Clippers through after an OT win over Minnesota
SEC Media Days open Monday in Tampa - Lane Kiffin's first appearance as LSU's coach headlines a six-new-coach class
Seahawks training camp opens to the public July 25 in Renton

deepDive.title: Guaranteed Money: Why NFL Contracts Are Read Like Callable Bonds, Not Bond Coupons
content: Tennessee's new deal with Jeffery Simmons is being reported as "three years, $105.8 million," but the number that actually matters to his agent, and to the Titans' cap planners, is the $100 million guaranteed inside it. That distinction sits at the center of today's brief in a way that echoes the fixed-income world Chris is heading into: just as bond investors learn to ignore a coupon rate and focus on yield to worst, NFL analysts learn to ignore the topline contract value and focus on the guarantee - because that's the only part of the number the team cannot walk away from.

The mechanism is structural. Unlike NBA or MLB deals, which are fully guaranteed for their stated length, NFL contracts are only guaranteed to the extent the team explicitly promises - split between injury guarantees, skill guarantees, and full guarantees that typically "vest" a year or two into the deal. A team can release a player the moment his non-guaranteed years begin without owing the remaining topline number, the same way a bond issuer can call in debt early once it's economically favorable to do so. Simmons's $100 million guaranteed through 2030 is Tennessee pre-committing to not exercise that option for most of the deal's life - which is exactly why agents fight over the guarantee figure, not the year-three number nobody expects to be paid in full.

This gap between headline value and true commitment is easy to miss because leagues and media report the bigger number by convention. The tell is in how often "record-breaking" contracts get quietly restructured or voided in year two or three once the guaranteed portion runs out - the player's real floor was always smaller than the press release implied. Chris Jones's $31.8 million-a-year defensive tackle mark, which Simmons's deal just eclipsed, is itself a useful anchor: comparing the guarantee-to-total ratio across those two deals says more about how much negotiating leverage each player actually had than the average annual value ever could.

The same logic is now migrating into college sports, which matters given today's transfer portal activity from Louisville, Kansas, and Duke. As NIL collectives and revenue-sharing deals start to look more like employment contracts, expect the next fight in college athletics to be exactly this one - not the total value of a package, but how much of it is actually guaranteed if a player gets hurt, loses a starting job, or a coach who recruited him leaves. Whether it's an NFL cap sheet or a college roster-building budget, the analytical habit is the same: read past the topline number to the commitment underneath it.
